metric_rationale:
This is a within-subject, parameter-free contrast that isolates the one-reason signature of Take-The-Best while cancelling out each subject's overall noise level.

For every trial I recompute (a) the TTB winner (first discriminating cue in descending-validity feature order) and (b) the tally winner. Trials split into CONFLICT trials, where the two heuristics point to different options (design trials 1, 2, 7, 8, 9, 10), and AGREEMENT trials, where they point to the same option (trials 5, 6, 11, 12). Tally-tie pairs (3, 4) are dropped because they are uninformative for this particular contrast. The metric is P(choose the TTB-favoured option | conflict) minus P(choose the TTB-favoured option | agreement).

Predictions:
- Take-The-Best: choice probability for the top-cue winner is sigmoid(beta) softened by the lapse, identically on every decisive pair regardless of tally margin or conflict status. So the two rates are the same and the metric is exactly 0 in expectation, for ALL values of beta and epsilon. Only binomial sampling noise (48 vs 32 trials per class) contributes, giving a tight per-subject variance of roughly 0.013.
- Tallying: on conflict trials the subject systematically chooses AGAINST the TTB option (rate 1 - q), while on agreement trials they choose WITH it (rate q). The metric is therefore strongly negative, around -0.6 to -0.9 for any moderately decisive beta, with modest across-subject spread driven mostly by the lapse rate.

Because the TTB prediction is a hard zero that does not depend on the fitted nuisance parameters, and the Tallying prediction is a large negative number, the two theories should separate by roughly 0.7-0.8 with small per-subject variance on both sides. It is not trivially true for TTB in the sense of being a restatement of the model: any strategy that weights evidence compensatorily (tallying, weighted-additive, or even partial cue integration) will push the score negative, while pure one-reason decision making pins it at zero.

The design contains pairs where the highest-validity cue (f5, or f2 after f5/f0 tie) points one way while the feature tally points the other way with a margin of at least 2 (trials 1, 2, 3, 9, 10). Restricting to margin>=2 conflicts guarantees that Tallying is confident (softmax on a tally difference of 2-4 saturates for almost all beta in the allowed range), so Tallying predicts choice of the tally winner at rate (1-eps)*sigmoid(margin*beta)+eps/2, typically ~0.85-1.0. Take-The-Best predicts exactly the opposite option at rate (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta)+eps/2, so its tally-consistency rate is typically ~0.0-0.15. The metric is a simple proportion over 40 pooled trials per subject, so binomial noise is small, and the only between-subject spread comes from the lapse parameter eps (bounded contribution <= 0.25). This yields a mean gap of roughly 0.7-0.75 with per-subject variance on the order of 0.01, which is far beyond what N=25 needs. It is not trivially true for Tallying: it is a directional prediction on genuinely conflicting evidence, and any subject who consults more than one reason but weights cues (e.g., weighted-additive) would also land high, while a strict one-reason decider lands low.

Take-The-Best must decide these trials on the single top-validity cue, which sits at screen position 3 (validity .95). On trial pairs 1-2 the two screen-EXTREME cues (position 0 = .70 and position 5 = .85) favour the option that the top-validity middle cue opposes. TTB therefore chooses the position-3 option on essentially every such trial (rate = (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta)+eps/2, expected ~0.85 across the parameter range, and never below 0.5). The read-order scanning model, by contrast, chooses the OPPOSITE option under BOTH orientations: a primacy reader anchors on position 0 (rank 0, weight ratio > e^2.1 over position 3 even at maximum validity pull gamma=.25), and a recency reader anchors on position 5 (highest rank). So the scanner's rate is ~eps/2 + sigmoid noise, i.e. ~0.03, and crucially it is the SAME (~0.03) for primacy and recency subjects, so the population mixture does not inflate between-subject variance. The metric selects these trials structurally (top cue discriminates, positions 0 and 5 both discriminate in the opposite direction) rather than by hard-coded trial index, works identically on pooled and single-subject data, and yields a mean gap of roughly 0.82 with small per-subject variance on both sides.

The design contains 'double dissociation' cells (pairs 1,2,7,8) where TTB's cue cascade (pos2 then pos3) points one way while BOTH primacy and recency read-order scanners are dominated by the screen extremes and point the other way. The metric automatically detects those cells (TTB winner opposite to the choice implied by both a positive-lambda and a negative-lambda position gradient) and reports the proportion of TTB-consistent responses there. Under Take-The-Best this is essentially sigmoid(beta) reduced by lapse (high, ~0.85 on average, tight because it is the same quantity on every such trial). Under read-order scanning it must be near 0 for EVERY subject regardless of their orientation, because the orientation-dependent bimodality is deliberately excluded (only cells where both orientations agree against TTB are counted). That makes the between-theory gap large while keeping per-subject variance small, since no subject-level parameter (lambda sign, gamma) can move the scanning prediction across the cut.

This isolates the 'both-orientations-agree' cell (trial pairs 1 and 2: d = +-[1,-1,-1,1,0], with the 90% expert tied) and scores the proportion of those trials on which the subject chose the option supported by screen positions 0 and 3 rather than positions 1 and 2.

Why it discriminates: under read-order scanning, the earliest discriminating cue (position 0) AND the latest discriminating cue (position 3) both favour the SAME option, so primacy readers and recency readers alike produce normalised evidence S strongly favouring that side (|S| ~ .45-.94, P ~ .97-1.00). There is no orientation escape hatch, so this cell is tight both within and across the competitor's whole parameter box, including its bimodal lambda sign - the classic source of between-subject variance for that theory is neutralised here.

Under the advocated threshold-terminated integrator, no partial margin ever reaches the sufficiency bar (max partial |E| = .235 < phi * w4 ~ .38), so the list is exhausted, the trial ends unresolved, and choice is a shallow softmax on a residual margin of w0 - w1 - w2 + w3 ~ -.06, i.e. a mild preference for the OPPOSITE (positions 1-2) side: expected value ~ .35-.45.

So the predicted values are roughly .38 (advocated) vs .98 (competitor) - opposite sides of chance, with small per-subject binomial noise over 16 trials per subject. The direction of the effect (and not merely its size) is diagnostic, and the metric is well-defined on both the pooled frame and a single subject's slice.

This metric isolates the two trial families (pairs 5/6 and 7/8) where the two theories make maximally opposed, orientation-robust predictions. In these items the first-read 0.78 expert and the last-read 0.56 expert (plus, in pairs 5/6, the 0.66 expert) all favour one option, while the single highest-validity 0.95 expert sitting mid-list favours the other. Under read-order scanning, ANY reader type follows the position-weighted, normalised evidence: primacy readers are anchored by the leading cue, recency readers by the last cue, so BOTH orientations select the first/last-favoured option at near-ceiling rate (~0.9-1.0), giving a tight, unimodal per-subject distribution with essentially no between-subject spread. Under threshold-terminated compensatory integration, the leading cues can never clear the sufficiency bar (max unread weight is the 0.95 expert's 0.34), the 0.95 cue itself cannot stop search, and the trial ends with a small unresolved residual that points the OTHER way (pairs 7/8, P~0.2-0.35) or is near chance (pairs 5/6, P~0.36-0.50). So the metric should be ~0.9+ under the advocated theory and ~0.3-0.4 under the competitor, with low variance under both because the direction is fixed across the whole parameter box for both orientations and there is no discrete strategy split in these cells. Pooling 32 trials per subject keeps binomial noise small.

This isolates the design's sharpest within-subject dissociation: trials 5/13 (L=0) and 6/14 (L=3) share the EXACT same difference vector d = (+1,0,-1,0,0,+1) up to side-mirroring \u2014 two mid-validity cues (screen positions 0 and 5) against the single 95% cue at position 2. They differ only in the number of shared positive endorsements, which discriminate nothing.

The metric is P(choose the 2-cue side | dense display) - P(choose the 2-cue side | sparse display), pooled over both mirror orientations so any side bias cancels.

Competing theory (read-order scanning): its evidence S = sum(w*d)/sum(w*|d|) is a function of d and screen position ONLY. Shared 1s are invisible to it, so it is mathematically forced to give the identical choice probability in both cells, for every lam, gamma, beta, epsilon and for both primacy and recency orientations. Predicted value: 0 (only binomial noise). Its per-subject variance is small because both proportions sit near the same ceiling and their sampling errors are of the same modest size (~12 trials each).

Advocated theory: load flattens the diagnosticity exponent (rho_eff = rho/(1+cL)) and switches on supra-additive corroboration (delta_eff = delta*L/(1+L)), flipping the decision from the single strong cue to the 2-cue majority. Hand-computing at mid parameters gives P(2-cue side) ~ .10 at L=0 and ~ .88 at L=3, i.e. a metric value near +0.75 to +0.80, stable across the whole parameter box (the sign flip is robust to rho, alpha, lam, c).

So the expected contrast is roughly 0.78 vs 0.00 with per-subject SDs on the order of 0.1-0.15 \u2014 a very large, tight separation at N=25. It is not trivially true for my theory: it is a genuine empirical claim that adding informationally irrelevant shared endorsements reverses which option people pick.

Cells 1-4 of the design are single-discriminating-cue trials: exactly one expert distinguishes the two products, and that expert is either weak (pos1 v=.56, pos4 v=.62) or strong (pos0 v=.72, pos3 v=.95). Under READ-ORDER SCANNING the relative-evidence term is S = sum(w*d)/sum(w*|d|) = +/-1 EXACTLY whenever a single cue discriminates, for every lambda, gamma and reader orientation. Hence choice probability is sigmoid(beta) (~.93-1.00 after lapse) identically for weak and strong cues: the strong-minus-weak accuracy difference must be ~0 (a mathematically forced null, not a fitted prediction). Under ANCHORED COMPENSATORY INTEGRATION with only PARTIAL normalisation (psi~.2-.4), the evidence on a single-cue trial is E = w_j^(1-psi), which scales with the cue's convex diagnosticity: hand-computing the competitor's own equations over its whole parameter box gives P(correct) ~ .53-.60 for pos1, ~.58-.65 for pos4, but ~.93-.97 for pos0 and ~.99 for pos3. So the metric should land near 0 for scanning and near +0.38-0.42 for the competitor. Both sides use 16 trials per subject and both theories are near-deterministic given parameters, so per-subject variance is small (scanning: only lapse/binomial noise; competitor: modest parameter jitter), giving a large mean gap with tight per-subject spread. Taking the strong-minus-weak DIFFERENCE also cancels any common attention/lapse level, so it isolates the flat-ceiling vs. validity-ladder signature (full vs partial per-trial normalisation) rather than overall accuracy.

The metric is the proportion of choices consistent with the option favoured by the two screen-extreme experts (position 0, v=.72 and position 5, v=.70) restricted to the two design cells where the competing read-order scanning model makes the SAME prediction for primacy and recency readers (so it is unimodal across subjects, no bimodality inflating between-subject variance): cell 5 (d = +1,0,-1,0,0,+1) and cell 8 (d = +1,-1,-1,-1,0,+1), plus their side mirrors. Under scanning, normalised evidence S is ~.73-.97 for primacy readers and ~.96-.98 for recency readers in both cells, so P(extreme-favoured) is near ceiling (~.90-.98 after lapses) for every subject. Under the advocated read-until-sufficient model with mildly compressed diagnosticity and a convex read-out, the mid-list .95 expert almost exactly offsets the two extremes in cell 5, and the convex kappa read-out crushes the residual |R|~.02-.09 to a coin flip (P~.50-.55); in cell 8 the dense mid-list crowd (.60/.95/.86) outweighs the two extremes and triggers a sufficiency stop at R~-.47, giving P(extreme-favoured)~.28-.35. Pooling 24 trials per subject (12 per cell) yields ~.42 for the advocated model vs ~.94 for scanning, with tight per-subject binomial + parameter noise (SD~.10 and ~.05 respectively), which is easily separable at N=25.  It is not trivially true of my theory: it depends jointly on the compression exponent, the sufficiency stop and the convex read-out, and any weighted-additive or lexicographic account with validity-driven weights could land anywhere on it.

The design's cell 5 (pairs 9/10, d = [+1,0,-1,-1,0,+1] and its mirror) is the one place where the two theories predict OPPOSITE choices over their entire parameter boxes, and where BOTH read-order orientations (primacy and recency) agree, so the advocated theory stays unimodal and tight rather than splitting into subpopulations. Under read-order scanning, the first-read (.62) and last-read (.58) cues dominate whichever orientation the subject has, giving normalised evidence S strongly positive for the extreme-favoured option (P ~ .67-1.00, typically ~.85+). Under read-until-sufficient integration, the leading .62 cue cannot clear the sufficiency bar set by the unread .95 expert, so the reader continues, the two mid-list heavyweights dominate, and with only 2/6 experts silent the silence discount barely bites: P(extreme-favoured option) ~ .18-.25. The metric is the proportion of these 12 trials per subject on which the extreme-endorsed option was chosen: expected ~0.85 for scanning vs ~0.22 for the competitor, with per-subject variance dominated by binomial noise over 12 trials (~0.01-0.02), so Welch's test at N=25 should be decisively significant. It is not trivially true for my theory: it is a directional prediction about which cues drive choice, which the competitor makes an equally strong opposite prediction about.

The design contains three cells whose predicted choice proportions move in opposite directions under the two theories. Cell 4 (pairs 7/8, d=[+1,0,-1,-1,+1]): the competitor's deadlock salience gate opens at full force and drives P(pro-extreme)~.88, while the read-until-sufficient model stops on the mid-list .95 expert and gives ~.31. Cell 8 (pairs 15/16): the competitor fires its saturating majority bonus (~.89) while the convex read-out crushes a near-balanced R to near indifference (~.47-.68). Cell 5 (pairs 9/10): the sufficiency stop makes the advocated model commit categorically (~.90) whereas the competitor integrates to a near-null vote (~.61). Summing the two cells where the competitor is higher and subtracting the cell where the advocated model is higher yields an index of roughly -0.0 for the advocated theory versus ~+1.16 for the competitor - a gap of over one unit. Each component rate is estimated from 12 trials per subject and all three components are strongly parameter-insensitive within each theory's stated parameter box, so per-subject variance stays small (dominated by binomial noise, ~0.02-0.03 per component), giving a very large Welch t at N=25. Crucially the index is not trivially true for either theory: it is a signed combination of directional choice proportions that either theory could in principle produce at any value.

The design contains two cells where the two accounts predict OPPOSITE choices, and each cell is presented twice (base + side-mirror) x 6 reps = 24 trials per subject, so a simple proportion has small binomial noise.

Cell 4 (d = [+1,-1,-1,0,0,0,+1]; the two .70 screen-extreme experts vs. the mid-list .95 and .86 heavyweights, three both-1 silent): the advocated reason-counting model is at an exact vote deadlock (kA = kB = 2), which opens its salience gate to full force, so the first/last screen rows decide and it picks the extremes-backed option with P ~ .73-.85. The read-until-sufficient competitor weights by compressed validity x a primacy-only attention profile, reads on past the deadlock and lands on a clearly negative relative evidence R ~ -.5, giving P ~ .29 for that same option.

Cell 8 (d = [-1,-1,+1,+1,+1,0,+1]; leading .70 expert and the .95 oracle favour one side, four later experts the other, only one silent feature so neither model's silence machinery is engaged): the advocated model's near-linear vote plus saturating majority bonus favours the four-expert side at P ~ .75-.82; the competitor accumulates a large early lead from the first two (heavily attention-weighted) positions, clears its sufficiency bar, commits on R = -1 and gives P ~ .05 for the four-expert side.

The metric is the proportion of choices, over those 24 trials, that agree with the option the advocated theory favours. Predicted values: ~0.78 under reason-counting-with-salience-gate vs. ~0.17 under read-until-sufficient integration -- a ~0.6 gap. Because the cells are mirrored across sides, side bias cannot inflate or deflate the score, and because both cells sit far from indifference in both models the per-subject variance is dominated by binomial noise over 24 trials (~0.007) plus modest parameter jitter, which should keep Welch's t large at N = 25.

The design's three 'direction-disagreement' cells (EXT, AUTH, TAIL) were constructed so that the advocated attention-lottery model, via asymmetric screen salience plus authority-contingent first-mismatch capture, follows the TOP screen row (position 0, validity .82) almost deterministically (P ~ .90-.93 per cell), while the competing reason-counting model integrates the full validity-weighted vote over all discriminating experts and therefore goes the OTHER way in EXT and AUTH (P(top-row option) ~ .18-.22) and is essentially at chance in TAIL (~ .47). The metric is simply the proportion of choices, restricted to those six displays (3 cells x 2 mirror orders, 36 trials per subject), that agree with the option favoured by the first discriminating screen row. Predicted values: ~0.90 under the advocated theory, ~0.29 under the competitor -- a ~60-point gap. Because it pools 36 trials per subject and both theories make near-extreme, parameter-robust predictions in these cells (the design rationale states the direction holds across both full parameter boxes), the per-subject sampling variance is small (binomial var ~0.002-0.007 plus modest parameter jitter), so the contrast should survive Welch's test at N=25. Mirroring A/B across the six displays removes any side-bias confound, and the metric is well defined on both pooled and single-subject slices.

The metric is the proportion of trials, pooled over two hand-picked stimulus cells (identified by content so that mirrored A/B presentations are collapsed), on which the subject chooses a designated 'focal' option.

Cell V1 ([1,0,1,0,1,0] vs [0,1,1,1,1,1]): the focal option is backed only by the top screen row (.74) while the two most valid experts (.95 at row 2 and .86 at row 4) plus a numerical majority oppose it. The advocated reason-counting model integrates ALL discriminating experts with near-linear validity weights and adds a saturating majority bonus, so it decisively rejects the focal option (P(focal) ~ .08). The attention-lottery model samples only k=2-3 rows drawn with weights strongly biased to the top of the panel and heavily discounted for the low-salience mid rows, so it mostly never reads the .95/.86 evidence and chooses the focal option most of the time (P(focal) ~ .70).

Cell AUTH ([1,1,0,1,0,0] vs [0,1,1,1,1,1]): the .95 and .86 experts are mute (mutual endorsements), so the top speaking row (.74) is the most diagnostic speaker and triggers the competitor's authority-contingent first-mismatch capture, driving it to follow that top row and pick the focal (P(focal) ~ .83). The advocated model computes its authority cap over ALL later rows including the silent .95 expert, so its first-cue commitment is suppressed; it instead counts three cheap dissenting reasons plus the majority bonus and rejects the focal (P(focal) ~ .17).

Both cells push in the SAME direction across theories (advocated low, competitor high), so averaging them roughly doubles the contrast while averaging over 24 trials per subject keeps binomial noise small (~.07 SD). Expected values: ~0.13 under the advocated theory versus ~0.77 under the attention lottery — a ~0.64 gap with tight per-subject spread. Crucially the metric is not trivially true for either model: it is a plain choice proportion on two ordinary stimulus pairs, and either model could in principle land anywhere in [0,1].

Composite of three within-subject contrasts whose predicted directions all add up under my (advocated) model and all point the other way under the competitor.

(1) ORACLE-0 cells (lone .95 expert at row 2 speaks, all other rows mutually ABSENT): my reversible silence term drives c NEGATIVE (eta*f_sil^q*vbar > 1 across the whole box), so the lone near-oracle endorsement is followed BELOW chance (~.27). The competitor's silence term is floored at c_min>0, so it must follow ABOVE chance (~.57) for every parameter setting.

(2) LONE-WEAK cell (only the .58 expert at row 4 speaks): the competitor adds a categorical unanimity bonus with a high-c panel and a tiny lapse, predicting confident following (~.80); I have no unanimity term and a large lapse, predicting near-chance following (~.55).

(3) TOP/BOTTOM READING SWAP cells (rows 0/1 vs rows 5/6 sign-exchanged with validity matched): the competitor's salience is symmetric, so its vote, salience sum and reason counts are analytically identical in the two cells and it is forced to ~.50 for the top-favoured option; my graded reading-attention multiplier pushes choices toward the option endorsed by the SCREEN-TOP rows (~.61).

Scoring follow(oracle-0) + follow(weak) - P(top-favoured) yields ~0.20 under my theory and ~0.87 under the competitor. Each component averages over 12-24 trials per subject and each is bounded in [0,1], so per-subject variance stays modest while the between-theory gap is ~0.67.

Two mechanistically opposite predictions are combined into a single difference-of-differences, so that the two theories land on opposite signs.

(1) Silence-composition cliff at FIXED difference vector (trials 13-16, d=[+1,-1,0,0,0,+1,+1], 3 silent rows either mutual endorsements or mutual abstentions). The advocated model has a SHARP sigmoid silence threshold at f0~.36 with mutual endorsements down-weighted by omega~.82: omega*3/7=.351 sits just below the threshold while 3/7=.429 sits just above, so its read-out gain collapses from c~.51 to the floor c_min=.10 and P(majority option) falls from ~.83 to ~.58 (a ~25-point drop produced by ratings that discriminate nothing). The competitor's smooth, power-law silence term moves c only .89 -> .80, giving a ~2-point drop. So silence_cliff ~ +.25 (advocated) vs ~ +.02 (competitor).

(2) Lone-oracle composition reversal (trials 7-10, only the .95 expert at row 1 discriminates; the other six rows are all mutual 0s or all mutual 1s). For the advocated model f_sil is far above its threshold in BOTH cells and eta*vbar>1, so c is FLOORED at c_min in both: it is analytically forced to give the same choice probability (~.57, above chance thanks to the categorical unanimity bonus). The competitor's REVERSIBLE silence term passes negative for the all-abstain version (c ~ -.35, predicting choice AGAINST the lone oracle, P~.31) but stays positive for the all-endorse version (c ~ +.19, P~.61). So oracle_reversal ~ 0 (advocated) vs ~ +.30 (competitor).

Subtracting gives ~ +0.25 under the advocated theory and ~ -0.29 under the competitor: a ~0.54 gap with opposite signs. Each of the four cells is estimated from 12 trials per subject (2 mirrored pairs x 6 reps), all contrasts are within-subject and side-balanced, so per-subject noise (sd~0.27) is small relative to the between-theory gap at N=25.

The design contains two families of displays. DENSE / high-evidence-mass cells (C: 4-1 majority; E: edge-deadlock; H: cheap coalition vs lone oracle) are exactly where the competitor's ABSOLUTE read-out, categorical saturating majority bonus and large constant residual salience (g_res~.25 in absolute units) push it to near-ceiling decisiveness (~.97/.94/.84), whereas DCRI-3s divides drive by the total speaking diagnosticity (relative read-out), gives the near-oracle a top-end premium that blunts the cheap coalition, and applies a difficulty-scaled lapse, so it stays much lower (~.89/.83/.64). SPARSE cells (A/B: lone-oracle vs .66 amid four mute rows; G1: 2-vs-1 with three mute endorsements; F: dk=1 numerosity cell) are where the competitor's sharp silence sigmoid floors confidence at c_min and its weaker commitment read-out leaves it near chance (~.56/.56/.67/.50), while DCRI-3s's smooth power-law silence discount plus strong commitment read-out and sqrt-numerosity keep it clearly above chance (~.69/.60/.78/.59).

The metric is the WITHIN-SUBJECT difference: (rate of choosing the designated favored option in DENSE cells) minus (same rate in SPARSE cells). Because it is a difference of two rates computed inside the same subject, subject-level decisiveness jitter (beta, lapse, overall gain) largely cancels, keeping between-subject variance small, while the theories' predicted crossover in the sign/size of the dense-vs-sparse gap is large: competitor ~ +0.34, DCRI-3s ~ +0.12. Mirrored pairs are included with flipped favored side, so any side bias cancels exactly.

Two within-subject, validity-matched contrasts that the two accounts order very differently, averaged to cut binomial noise.

(1) SILENCE-CLIFF / DISSENTER CONTRAST (cell 3 minus cell 2). Cell 2 is a 3-0 unanimous display with four mutual-endorsement (1,1) rows; cell 3 is identical except the cheap pos5 expert now dissents (3-1, three mute rows). The advocated model has a SHARP silence sigmoid (f0~0.36) with mutual endorsements weighted omega~0.82: cell 2 sits above the cliff (effective silence .469) so confidence collapses to ~.11 and P(majority)~.65, whereas cell 3 falls just below the cliff (.351) so confidence jumps to ~.65 and P(majority)~.90. Hand computation at central parameters gives +0.24, and even at the unfavourable corners of the parameter box the sign stays positive. DCRI-3s uses a SMOOTH power-law silence discount plus a RELATIVE read-out, so its drive drop and confidence rise cancel almost exactly: .803 -> .800, i.e. ~0.00. Note the level ordering also reverses (DCRI is 15 pts above the advocate in cell 2 and 10 pts below in cell 3), so no validity-only or side-bias account can mimic this.

(2) SATURATING-MAJORITY / EDGE CONTRAST (cell 6 minus cell 7). Cell 6 pits the oracle (.96) plus .86 against three cheap/mid experts (2-3); cell 7 adds exactly one more cheap dissenter at the bottom screen edge (2-4). For the advocated model this single row simultaneously switches on the categorical saturating majority bonus (-0.67) and adds a full edge-salience unit at the residual gate, flipping P(oracle side) from ~.63 to ~.21 (a 42-point, direction-reversing swing). DCRI's sqrt numerosity, compressive validity map with an oracle premium and growing relative denominator produce only ~.507 -> .399 (11 points). This contrast involves essentially no silence machinery, so it is robust to the parameters that drive contrast (1).

Composite prediction: advocated ~0.33, DCRI ~0.05. Each cell contributes 12 trials per subject, so per-subject binomial variance of the average contrast is ~0.015, tight enough for N=25 despite parameter jitter. The metric is well defined on a single subject's slice and on the pooled frame alike.
